sections.html:
Charleston is the county seat of Charleston County and the most populous city in South Carolina. The 2020 census counted 150,227 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 159,423. The metro area, which spans Berkeley, Charleston and Dorchester counties, had an estimated 849,417 people in 2023.

The city is not one market. The old downtown is the Peninsula, between the Ashley and Cooper rivers. City limits also take in West Ashley, James Island, Johns Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island. A house on the Peninsula and a house on Johns Island share a city name but face different rules, lot types and buyer pools.

Charleston was founded in 1670, so a lot of its housing is old, and old houses come with repair lists. An earthquake in 1886 damaged about 2,000 buildings, and Hurricane Hugo hit on September 21, 1989. Buyers and inspectors here look hard at foundations, roofs, wiring and past water damage.

If your house has deferred repairs, a traditional listing can drag. Buyers who need a mortgage often ask for repairs after the inspection, and some lenders balk at houses in poor shape. Demand in the city comes from job relocations, investors and second-home buyers, but a house in the wrong condition or the wrong flood zone is hard to place with an ordinary financed buyer.

Flood risk is the biggest condition issue for many Charleston houses. The city sits at about 3 feet of elevation, summer brings almost half the year's rain, and hurricanes threaten from summer into early fall.

The city runs a floodplain program with rules that matter at sale time. Any work inside a Special Flood Hazard Area needs a permit, including painting, interior finishes and storm-damage repairs. That area covers AE, Coastal A and VE zones, which have a 1 percent or greater annual chance of flooding. Rules owners should know:

  • Since July 1, 2020, new construction in the flood hazard area must be designed 2 feet above Base Flood Elevation, and residential substantial improvements must be 1 foot above it.
  • Slab-on-grade building types 1A, 1B, 2A and 3 are prohibited in the 100-year floodplain for projects applied for on or after January 1, 2024.
  • Coastal A Zone design rules have applied to new construction and substantial improvements since January 1, 2023.
  • FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 applied to new flood policies from October 1, 2021 and to renewals from April 1, 2022.

You can request elevation certificates and flood hazard information from floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. Ask before you set a price, because a buyer's flood insurance quote can change what they will pay. The city's floodplain management page and flood zone permit page have the details.

sections.h2: Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Charleston house?
sections.html:
Only in limited cases. The city sorts short-term rentals into categories by location, and each category limits a property to one rental unit.

  • Category 1 covers the Old and Historic District on the peninsula, for existing structures individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 covers the rest of the peninsula outside the overlay, for buildings constructed 50 or more years ago.
  • Category 3 covers areas off the peninsula, including Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

Every category requires one extra off-street parking space, 9 feet by 18 feet 6 inches, on top of the parking zoning already requires. A single-family home needs 3 spaces in total. Commercially zoned property in the overlay can seek a Commercial Short Term Rental Permit, and residentially zoned property can seek a Bed and Breakfast Permit. Questions go to shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov or 843-724-7311, and the category criteria page lays out the rules.

If your house has been rented short term, tell buyers what permit it holds. Anyone paying for rental income will want proof.

South Carolina charges $1.85 for each $500 of value, or any part of $500, under Code section 12-24-10. The split is below.

Who receives itFee per $500 of value
State$1.30
County$0.55
Total$1.85

The seller is liable for the fee, and the buyer is secondarily liable. A value affidavit is filed with the deed, and the register of deeds can waive it. Some transfers are exempt, including a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and the affidavit must then state the reason. The statute is posted at scstatehouse.gov. Charleston County sets its own recording and tax dates, so confirm them with the county offices.

sections.h2: Property tax and what changes after a sale
sections.html:
South Carolina taxes an owner-occupied legal residence at a 4 percent assessment ratio and other property at 6 percent. The 4 percent rate applies to the home and up to five contiguous acres, and the home cannot be rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year.

A buyer who will not live in the house usually loses the 4 percent rate, so the same house can carry a bigger bill after a sale to an investor. Counties must reassess property every fifth year, and owners must be notified of value changes of $1,000 or more (Code sections 12-43-217 and 12-43-220). Ask the county treasurer what is owed before closing so nothing surprises you at the table.

sections.h2: Choosing between a listing and a cash sale
sections.html:
Sellers here tend to run into the same few problems, and each points to a different sale route.

  • Flood-zone repairs that need a permit before work can start.
  • Older structures with deferred roof, plumbing or electrical work.
  • Inherited houses where the heirs must agree before anything is signed.
  • Rental houses where the tenant, the permit or both need sorting out.

A listing suits a house in good shape that can wait for showings. A cash sale suits a house where repairs, permits or a deadline make a long listing a poor fit. A cash buyer typically buys as-is, so you skip the repair negotiations, the appraisal and the wait on a buyer's loan approval.

Whichever route you pick, gather three things first: your flood zone and elevation certificate, the permit history for any work or rental use, and your mortgage payoff figure. If the house is inherited, bring the paperwork that shows who has authority to sign. Having these ready shortens the time between an offer and closing.

faqs.q: What is the main flood rule when I sell a house in Charleston?
faqs.a: The city requires a permit for any work in a Special Flood Hazard Area, including repairs after storm damage. Since July 1, 2020, residential substantial improvements there must sit 1 foot above Base Flood Elevation. Ask the floodplain office for your elevation certificate before you price the house.

faqs.q: How is the South Carolina deed fee figured on a Charleston sale?
faqs.a: It is $1.85 per $500 of value, or any part of it, with $1.30 going to the state and $0.55 to the county. By statute the seller is liable and the buyer is secondarily liable. Your closing attorney will give you the exact figure.

faqs.q: Can I rent my Charleston house short term after buying it?
faqs.a: Maybe. Each of the city's three categories allows one short-term rental unit per property plus an extra parking space. Categories 1 and 2 depend on location and building age on the peninsula. Confirm with the city before you count on rental income.

faqs.q: Does selling to a cash buyer change flood or permit duties?
faqs.a: No. Disclosure, permits and the deed fee apply however the house sells. A cash sale can skip buyer financing delays and repair requests, and that is the practical difference for most Charleston sellers.

faqs.q: Where can I find Charleston County tax dates?
faqs.a: Start with the county auditor, assessor and treasurer. South Carolina law sets January 15 as the last day to pay without penalty on most bills, but notices and appeal windows vary by cycle, so call the offices directly.
